Among some Americans, the Civil War is a perennially favorite topic. Imagine my amusement when I found a compendium of anecdotes. Of course, I had to share it with this community. Let me skip to the anecdote before I indulge my verbose proclivities.

Became a soldier after all

Mrs. Crissey, of Decatur, Illinois, whose husband was chaplain in an Illinois regiment, related to a visitor that many years ago her little baby, while playing in the street, fell down, and began to cry.

A very tall young man, who was just then passing by with a yoke of oxen, picked the child up, and handing him inside the gate, said, cheerily,"You will never make a soldier if you cry for that."

The little fellow at once banished his grief.

The tall young man was Abraham Lincoln, and Mrs. Crissey introduced to the visitor a young Captain, home on furlough, as her son, who had become a soldier after all.

Such are the odds and ends which turn up with the whirligig of old Father Time.

If you like anecdotes, or you like the Civil War, this book is well worth checking out. It was written in 1866 and published in the Union stronghold of Ohio. The editor was Richard Millar Devens, who is best known for having coined the term "business intelligence" in his Cyclopædia of Commercial and Business Anecdotes of 1865. (Hint, hint, dear voaters...) Thus, a Union bias may be assumed but the range of plausibility is limited: these anecdotes had to be believable -- even to people who had witnessed the battles.

With this in mind, several points make astonishing reading: the burning of Southern cotton fields, the confiscation of weapons held by the families of Southern officers (the anecdote which highlights this relates to a sword -- and the editor concludes the story is a fiction), the role of German mercenaries (who were baffled by the password "Potomoc" which they rendered "buttermilk" and then oafishly communicated to the soldiers they had previously excluded), the pervasive racism.

So, did Lincoln really give these words of encouragement? Who knows. The anecdote contains ranks, names, and states which is more than can be said for many of these short tales. Fortunately, for the preservation of the anecdote, it is connected with a famous personage. Indeed, that is about all the tale trades on.

While I like the article as a call to attention that there is a problem, I would have liked to see more opinion and analysis. As I see it, there are several conflating factors that exacerbate the problem of police aggression:

  • People want to live in safe areas, so they support increasing power and aggressive capability of their police forces. No candidates for public office want to be accused of being "soft on crime."
  • The police are bolstered by the war on terror through hand-me-down materiel and (in many cases) an influx of veterans to fill positions. While the demands of stability operations abroad and policing at home are similar, there are key differences that need to be addressed through re-training and service culture.
  • In an effort to reduce taxes, many communities rely more upon court fees and penalties. All the more reason to be aggressive in the prosecution of even minor offenses.
  • The funds are limited. Without an expressed desire to have more face-to-face interactions, police will remain in their cruisers so they can patrol a larger area and won't exit the cruiser except to respond to an infraction of the law. If most interactions are inherently inflammatory (as there is an implicit accusation of criminality for the police to initiate interaction), then the officer learns to treat all interactions that way. This works for the residents of the area as well: If a police officer's presence implies an accusation, then their very presence (or at least their attention) is an offense to that person. Aggression naturally begets aggression.
  • As the US population becomes more urbanized, more areas grow to become patchworks of independent municipalities. While seemingly a minor concern, at a least a certain portion of the police force of an area should be from that community. The absence of this humanizing context for the police reduces their ability to control a situation with anything but fear.

This is certainly not an exhaustive list of problems--or even a well-researched one. As always, there are a litany of issues arising from the perennial quandary of "Who will watch the watchers?" But, I feel that the issue is systemic and is mired by a number of issues, which would take time to tease out and remedy. To that end, I would like to see more public criticism of the police and particularly police culture rather than wrapping them into a "hero" category with military and firefighters. I respect these careers and recognise an innate "defender" status, but exalting them as de facto heroes seems excessive, especially when it's used to stifle any criticism.
